stories.title: Heathrow expansion an 'outdated' risk, mayor says
stories.summary: The London mayor has formally opposed plans for a third runway at Heathrow Airport, arguing the expansion threatens environmental targets and transport networks. City Hall and Transport for London (TfL) submitted a joint response to the government's draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS) consultation. Sir Sadiq Khan claimed the strategic case relied on outdated evidence that "fails to reflect current climate laws and travel habits". The government said it was reviewing the response, while Heathrow questioned many of the claims made in City Hall's submission. The airport said the expansion was the "most important economic growth opportunity available to the UK". But Sir Sadiq said he saw no evidence the proposals were compatible with a credible path to net zero. "The evidence suggests Heathrow expansion is a risk that we simply cannot afford to take." City Hall said additional flights could reverse the progress in reducing air pollution in communities surrounding Heathrow brought by the Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez). "The whole case for Heathrow expansion relies on outdated evidence that fails to take into account the urgent challenges we face today," Sir Sadiq said. "I will continue to vehemently oppose these plans as I seek to build a fairer, safer, greener, more prosperous London for everyone." Heathrow Airport Limited is preparing plans for a new 2.1 mile (3.5km) northwest runway - which would require realigning a section of the M25 - with a final decision expected following a parliamentary vote in 2029. A spokesperson for the airport rejected claims that expansion was incompatible with net zero goals - and said the airport was committed to a completely privately-funded noise insulation scheme for local homes.

stories.title: Rubio urges allies to isolate Nicaragua's 'brutal dictatorship' after vote to ban opposition parties
stories.summary: Ortega hit back at Washington dismissing US pressure while the reform - which also extends presidential terms to seven years - still requires a second legislative vote before taking effect in January. Nicaragua's ruling elite tightened its grip on power this week after the country's National Assembly voted to bar opposition parties from future elections, a move US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denounced as the final collapse of the country's democratic pretences. Tuesday's vote was only the first of two required approvals: Nicaraguan law requires constitutional amendments to clear two separate legislative sessions before taking effect, and co-president. Rosario Murillo has said the second vote will begin on January 18. Rubio said the vote confirmed that Nicaragua's elections could no longer be considered free or fair, describing the National Assembly as "captive" to President Daniel Ortega and his wife, Murillo. In a statement, he said the pair had used the reform to "entrench their illegitimate dynasty" and indefinitely deny Nicaraguans the chance to vote them out. He went further, calling on other nations to cut off routine dealings with Managua. "Dictatorships that deny the unalienable rights of their citizens should not enjoy the same economic or political benefits as governments committed to defending hemispheric peace and security," Rubio said, urging international partners to "immediately stop business as usual operations with this brutal dictatorship." Ortega hit back, without naming Rubio directly, casting the United States as an aggressor emboldened by its military strength. Speaking at an event marking the anniversary of the Nicaraguan army, he said: "Simply because it is a global military power, it feels entitled to attack." He added a defiant message to critics of his government: "To those who constantly threaten us, here you have a people and an army that will never be bought and never surrender." On 19 July, Ortega had already signalled the direction of travel, declaring publicly that "there won't be any more elections" in Nicaragua, a step he framed as necessary to stop the opposition from "seizing the government" again.

stories.title: South Korea utility proposes Samsung pays $18 billion in advance for power, paper says
stories.summary: KEPCO has proposed that Samsung Electronics pay 20 trillion won (S$18.69 billion) in advance for power supply until 2031 to fund grid expansion. KEPCO also suggested SK Hynix pay five trillion won in advance, aiming to support investments for semiconductor and AI data centres. The utility plans to use the funds to build power infrastructure and will pay interest above the yield on 2-year South Korean government bonds. Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) has proposed Samsung Electronics pay 20 trillion won (S$18.69 billion) in advance for power lasting until 2031 to help fund the expansion of its grid, the Chosun Ilbo reported on Sept 3. It has also proposed that SK Hynix pay five trillion won in advance, the newspaper said, citing an internal KEPCO document. State-run KEPCO, South Korea’s main utility, said in a statement it had suggested an advance payment scheme to major power users including Samsung and SK Hynix, but that participation, interest rates, payment amounts and payment periods had not been finalised. Samsung and SK Hynix declined to comment. KEPCO said the proposed arrangement was intended to help meet rising investment needs from semiconductor and AI data centre projects, while providing companies with more certainty over timely power supply for new factories.
